title: Wildfires and extreme heat show climate change is now Europe’s biggest security threat
gist: Chatham House reframes climate change as Europe's single biggest systemic security threat, documenting record-summer heat, drought and wildfire damage, arson as asymmetric warfare, and the diversion of militaries to disaster response. It argues climate adaptation should be reclassified as defence spending under NATO's 5%-of-GDP commitment, with adaptation returns of up to 6.35x avoided damages.

themes.theme: Climate as top systemic security risk

insights.claim: Climate change has become Europe's biggest systemic security risk because no other threat simultaneously affects so many countries, people and critical systems at once.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signals a policy reframing that could redirect defence budgets and resilience spending toward climate adaptation — watch for reclassification of climate as defence-related.
insights.quote: Climate change is now Europe’s biggest systemic security risk.

insights.claim: Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent and existing policies will not be sufficient to adapt to an expected 2.4°C to 3.9°C rise in global mean temperature this century.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Frames adaptation as a losing race — investors should expect persistent, escalating physical climate risk to European assets and insurance lines.
insights.quote: Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent.

insights.claim: Extreme heat contributed to an estimated 10,000 excess deaths during the June 2026 heatwave and destroyed roughly 9 million tonnes of crops from the European harvest.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Large crop loss is bullish for European agricultural commodity prices and a bearish signal for food-security-exposed regions.
insights.quote: an estimated 10,000 excess deaths during the June heatwave, which also destroyed roughly 9 million tonnes of crops

insights.claim: So far in 2026 over 600,000 hectares of land and forests have burned across almost the entire continent, forcing hundreds of thousands to evacuate.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Scale of burn area supports demand for firefighting assets, satellite monitoring and reinsurance repricing.
insights.quote: so far this year over 600,000 hectares of land and forests have burned

insights.claim: Falling river levels have forced nuclear reactors to shut down due to lack of suitable cooling water, threatening energy supply chains.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Climate-driven nuclear curtailment tightens power markets in heat events — a recurring bullish catalyst for European power prices and a reliability risk for nuclear-heavy grids.
insights.quote: Falling river levels have forced nuclear reactors to shut down due to a lack of suitable cooling water

themes.theme: Climate terrorism and arson as asymmetric warfare

insights.claim: Prolonged heat and drought turn countries into a 'tinderbox' where a single act of arson can trigger mass evacuations, destroy infrastructure and overwhelm emergency services, making wildfire a potential instrument of terrorism or asymmetric warfare.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Elevates arson to a national-security threat vector — watch for policy demand in wildfire surveillance, detection and prosecution capacity.
insights.quote: This makes wildfire a potentially devastating instrument of terrorism or asymmetric warfare.

insights.claim: France has arrested almost 500 people in 2026 on suspicion of starting fires, and as of 30 July the interior ministry said around 70 per cent of those detained were accused of deliberate arson.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Hard evidence that most fires are deliberate reframes wildfire risk from purely climatic to a preventable-crime problem — shifts where mitigation dollars go.
insights.quote: France has arrested almost 500 people on suspicion of starting fires; as of 30 July the interior ministry said around 70 per cent of those detained were accused of deliberate arson.

insights.claim: Russian drone strikes have repeatedly set forests ablaze in Ukraine, including multiple fires in the Chernobyl exclusion zone and Zhytomyr in May 2026.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Demonstrates fire being weaponized in active conflict — a live example of climate-conditions amplifying warfare tactics.
insights.quote: In May 2026, drone attacks caused multiple forest fires in the Chernobyl exclusion zone and Zhytomyr.

insights.claim: Militaries were deployed over 30 times in response to wildfires across Europe in June and July 2026 alone, diverting personnel and logistics away from other security threats.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Climate response is quietly consuming defence capacity — a structural readiness cost that argues for higher total defence-plus-resilience budgets.
insights.quote: militaries were deployed over 30 times in response to wildfires across Europe in June and July alone

insights.claim: Spain deployed more than 1,200 military personnel and 400 vehicles for a single major fire in July, while around 200 UK military personnel are currently fighting wildfires in south Wales.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Quantifies the per-event military footprint of climate disasters — a recurring drain that supports investment in dedicated civilian firefighting capacity.
insights.quote: In July, Spain deployed more than 1,200 military personnel and 400 vehicles for a single major fire.

insights.claim: Climate change undermines military readiness directly by damaging bases, airfields and transport networks, as when dry conditions caused wildfires at Netherlands military training grounds in April.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Physical climate risk to defence infrastructure adds a hardening/adaptation capex line to military budgets.

insights.claim: European NATO members have committed to spend 5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035, including up to 1.5 per cent on broader defence-related investment such as critical infrastructure and resilience.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The vaguely-defined 1.5% bucket is a potential funding channel — companies in resilience, infrastructure and civil protection could capture defence-budget flows.
insights.quote: European NATO members have committed to spend 5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035, including up to 1.5 per cent on broader investment related to defence and security

insights.claim: NATO recognizes climate change as a security threat but has not explicitly designated climate adaptation as defence-related spending; classifying it under the 1.5% bucket could help members meet spending commitments.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A policy catalyst to watch — reclassification would unlock large adaptation flows and blur the line between defence and climate infrastructure investment theses.
insights.quote: it has not explicitly designated climate adaptation as defence-related spending

insights.claim: The NATO Science and Technology Organization's January 2026 climate security assessment calls climate change a 'systemic problem' and says NATO's 2021 Climate Change and Security Action Plan should be thoroughly updated.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Institutional momentum inside NATO signals rising procurement and doctrine change around climate — an early indicator for defence-adjacent climate vendors.
insights.quote: climate change as a ‘systemic problem’ that impacts all other security risks

insights.claim: European policies have cut EU27 emissions to roughly 35 per cent below 1990 levels, but the EU27 still emits 3.2 gigatonnes of greenhouse gases annually, or six per cent of global emissions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Europe's shrinking but still-material emissions share underpins the argument for sustained decarbonization capex and its 'global signalling' influence on policy elsewhere.
insights.quote: the EU27 is still responsible for 3.2 gigatonnes of greenhouse gas emissions annually, or six per cent of global emissions

insights.claim: The EU needs to invest approximately €70 billion a year in climate adaptation until 2050, and the UK around £11 billion annually, to prevent the worst impacts.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Sizes a multi-decade adaptation market — a durable demand backdrop for infrastructure, engineering and resilience-tech providers.
insights.quote: the EU needs to invest approximately €70 billion a year in climate adaptation until 2050

insights.claim: Climate-related disasters caused an average of €45 billion in direct EU losses annually during 2020–2024, and inadequate adaptation could cost the UK £60-260 billion annually by 2050.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The cost-of-inaction dwarfs adaptation spend, strengthening the ROI case that could unlock public budgets and de-risk private adaptation investment.
insights.quote: Climate-related disasters caused a yearly average of €45 billion in direct EU losses during 2020–2024

insights.claim: Every euro invested in protection against coastal flooding can avoid around €6.35 in damages, per the European Commission's Joint Research Centre.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A concrete ~6x return figure is a persuasive lever for adaptation budgets and a benchmark for evaluating resilience-project economics.
insights.quote: every euro invested in protection against coastal flooding can avoid around €6.35 in damages

insights.claim: Climate adaptation should be understood not as an environmental expense but as a cost-effective and necessary investment in European national security and strategic autonomy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The core reframing — if adopted, it re-prices adaptation from ESG/environmental budgets to security budgets, a much larger pool.
insights.quote: Climate adaptation should therefore be understood not as an environmental expense, but as a cost-effective and necessary investment in European national security and strategic autonomy.
